title: Kestrel Pumps: a plant in Vietnam
prompt: Our client is Kestrel Pumps, a European manufacturer of industrial water pumps. It serves Southeast Asia entirely by exporting from its home plant, but freight and import tariffs eat into the margin, and regional demand is growing faster than the home plant can supply. The board is deciding whether to build a plant in Vietnam to serve the region locally, or to keep exporting. They have asked us to evaluate the decision.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 1 — Export economics, per pump
exhibits.unitsNote: US dollars per pump; the selling price is the same in both scenarios

exhibits.title: Exhibit 2 — Projected regional demand for Kestrel pumps
exhibits.unitsNote: Thousands of pumps per year; the home plant can supply at most 20K per year to the region

exhibits.title: Exhibit 3 — Vietnam plant, key assumptions
exhibits.unitsNote: The plant would be operational from the first year of the horizon

rows: One-off cost to build the plant

questions.prompt: Before structuring the analysis, what should we clarify with Kestrel first? Select the two most relevant.
options: Does the board have a financial hurdle for an investment of this size?
Can the home plant actually supply everything the region will demand?
What colour are the pumps painted for the Asian market?
How many patents does Kestrel hold in Europe?
What is the CEO’s favourite market to visit?

optionRationale: A must-have. A plant is a large, hard-to-reverse capital commitment; the case will be judged against whatever hurdle the board sets.
The binding constraint. If the home plant cannot serve future demand, "keep exporting" quietly means "give up growth", and the comparison changes shape.
Cosmetic specification has no bearing on where to build capacity.
Patent count does not change the export-versus-local-build economics.
Not a data point at all.
commonMistakes: Skipping the capacity question and comparing the two paths at today’s volume
Not asking for the hurdle the investment must clear

questions.followUp:
On the hurdle: the board wants the plant to pay back within four years of opening.

On capacity: the home plant can spare at most 20K pumps a year for Southeast Asia — its remaining output is committed to Europe. Regional demand is already above that and rising.

questions.prompt: Which areas would you investigate to compare exporting against building in Vietnam? Select the four most relevant.
options: Per-pump economics of each path — production cost, freight and tariffs
How regional demand develops over the horizon, against each path’s capacity
The investment cost of the plant and how fast it pays back
The history of Kestrel’s founding family
Risks of operating a first plant far from home — quality, currency, management
The typeface used in Kestrel’s regional advertising
European labour union reaction to opening a plant abroad

optionRationale: The unit economics are where tariffs and freight either justify the plant or do not.
Volume is half the profit equation, and the export path is capacity-capped — the comparison moves with demand.
The capex and the board’s payback hurdle are what the whole case is measured against.
Heritage is not a decision variable.
A first offshore plant is an operating-model change, not just a spreadsheet line; the risks belong in the structure.
Marketing cosmetics do not bear on a manufacturing footprint decision.
Worth managing later, but it is a stakeholder issue, not one of the four analyses that decide the economics.
commonMistakes: Structuring only the cost side and ignoring that the plant also unlocks volume the home plant cannot supply
Leaving out the risks of a first offshore operation

questions.followUp: Here are the export economics per pump. Work from these for the next question.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, what margin does Kestrel earn today on each pump it exports to Southeast Asia?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in dollars per pump, to the nearest dollar.

commonMistakes: Charging the tariff on cost rather than on the selling price
Forgetting the freight
Quoting the landed cost instead of the margin

questions.followUp:
So exporting earns $900 a pump — a 15% margin, with $600 of tariff and $300 of freight taken out of every unit before Kestrel sees a cent.

Now volume. Here is the demand projection; remember the home plant can supply at most 20K pumps a year to the region.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2 and the export margin you just calculated, what profit does the export path earn over the five years?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in $ millions, rounded to the nearest million.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Demand exceeds 20K in every year, so the export path sells its full 20K cap each year.
20,000 pumps × $900 = $18M a year.
Five years: $18M × 5 = $90M.
commonMistakes: Multiplying the margin by demand (150K pumps over the period) rather than by what the home plant can actually supply
Using a single year instead of the five-year total
Treating the 20K cap as a one-off rather than an annual limit

questions.followUp:
Exactly — the cap binds in every year, so exporting earns $90M over the period while total demand of 150K pumps goes largely unserved: rivals pick up the rest.

Here is what the Vietnam plant would look like.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 3, what margin would Kestrel earn on each pump built in Vietnam?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in dollars per pump, to the nearest dollar.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Cost per pump: $3,900 production + $100 regional freight = $4,000. No tariff.
Margin: $6,000 − $4,000 = $2,000 per pump.
commonMistakes: Still charging the 10% tariff, which local production avoids
Using the home plant’s freight figure
Deducting the $150M capex from the per-pump margin — it is a one-off, handled separately

questions.followUp: A $2,000 margin — a third of the selling price, against 15% when exporting. And the plant’s 40K capacity covers demand in every year, averaging 30K pumps a year over the horizon.

questions.prompt: What is the five-year profit of the Vietnam path, after the cost of building the plant?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in $ millions, rounded to the nearest million.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Average demand: 150K pumps over five years = 30K a year, all of it within the plant’s capacity.
Profit: 30,000 × $2,000 = $60M a year on average, $300M over five years.
Less the plant: $300M − $150M = $150M.
commonMistakes: Capping volume at 20K out of habit — the new plant’s capacity is 40K
Charging the $150M in every year instead of once
Comparing to zero rather than remembering exporting also earns $90M

questions.followUp: So the Vietnam path earns $150M over five years against $90M for exporting — a $60M gain, plus a structurally better margin from year six onward. The board’s test, though, was payback.

questions.prompt: The board asked for payback within four years. Measured against the profit Kestrel would otherwise have earned by exporting, how long does the plant take to pay back?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in years, to one decimal place — for four and a half years, type 4.5.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Incremental profit of the plant: $60M − $18M = $42M a year on average.
Payback: $150M ÷ $42M ≈ 3.6 years.
commonMistakes: Dividing by the plant’s full $60M profit instead of the incremental $42M — the export profit was already being earned
Using a single early year’s demand, which understates the average
Rounding to 4 and calling the hurdle failed — it is met with margin

questions.followUp: Payback in roughly 3.6 years clears the four-year hurdle. The economics favour building; what could still go wrong is the next question.

questions.prompt: What are the most relevant risks of Kestrel’s first plant outside Europe? Select the three most relevant.
options: Ramp-up risk — a new plant and workforce missing quality or volume targets in the early years
Currency risk — costs in dong, revenue across the region, and a home currency none of them match
Tariff policy risk — the trade rules that justify the plant could change again
Weather risk — European winters disrupting the home plant
Font licensing risk on regional packaging

optionRationale: Real and near-term: the payback case assumes full production from year one, which first plants rarely deliver.
Real and permanent: the case’s margins move with exchange rates the client does not control.
Real and structural: $600 of the per-pump advantage is tariff avoidance, and tariffs are set by governments, not by Kestrel.
The home plant’s weather exposure is unchanged by this decision.
commonMistakes: Missing that the tariff saving — the biggest single lever — is also the most fragile assumption
Ignoring ramp-up and assuming year-one output equals nameplate capacity

questions.followUp:
Ramp-up: stage the capacity, keep exporting in parallel during year one, and send an experienced home-plant team to run the start-up.

Currency: match costs and revenues where possible and hedge the gap.

Tariffs: the risk cuts both ways — tariffs could also rise, which would make exporting worse and the plant more valuable. Diversifying the footprint is itself a hedge.

questions.prompt: Kestrel’s CEO calls for your recommendation on the Vietnam plant. Please give your answer in seven to eight lines maximum.

keyPoints: Leads with the recommendation: build the plant
Gives the financial reason with numbers: $150M versus $90M over five years, and payback in about 3.6 years against a four-year hurdle
Explains the two drivers: margin per pump more than doubles ($900 to $2,000), and the plant serves demand the home plant must turn away
Notes the strategic upside: a regional footprint keeps growing in value after the horizon
Names the conditions: staged ramp-up with exports running in parallel, currency hedging, and monitoring of trade policy
Stays inside seven or eight lines and does not narrate the calculation
commonMistakes: Reciting the arithmetic instead of leading with the answer
Ignoring the capacity story and framing the plant as a pure cost play
Omitting ramp-up risk after the payback case assumed full year-one output

closing: That is the end of the case. Your transcript is ready — copy it into an LLM to be graded on what you actually said, not on what you meant.
